weekLabel: Week 11 · Meeting A · Optimization II: Nonlinear and Gradient-Based Search

slides.title: The computer finds a minimum. Which one, and why, is today's lesson.
slides.subtitle: scipy.optimize.minimize follows the slope downhill from a starting guess — initial guess, bounds, local optimum vs. global optimum
slides.teaching: Open by holding last week's Radley Hall roof LP result next to Week 9's two-basin heatmap. Ask: for a smooth, curved objective like this one, can we solve it exactly the way linprog solved the roof? Today's answer is no — we search instead, and the search can go wrong in a specific, predictable way that is the whole point of the lesson.

slides.title: Following the slope downhill does not always reach the lowest point
slides.statement: scipy.optimize.minimize starts at your initial guess and repeatedly steps toward lower values — but it only ever sees the slope right where it is standing.
slides.supporting: If your starting guess sits in the wrong basin, minimize slides confidently downhill into a real, comparable-looking trap and stops there — reporting success the entire way.
slides.teaching: Foreshadow the two demonstrations coming later this deck: the exact same function and bounds, two different starting guesses, two very different reported answers.

outcomes.head: Distinguish

outcomes.head: Explain
outcomes.body: State why the starting guess — not a bug, not bad luck — can change which optimum minimize reports.

slides.title: Objective function and bounds, recalled

left.head: Objective function
left.body: The one quantity you are trying to make as small (or as large) as possible. Last week it was roof benefit in dollars; this week it is energy_proxy(wwr, shade_m), a single nonlinear number combining both design variables.

right.head: Bounds
right.body: The allowed range for each design variable. Week 10 wrote bounds as a list of (min, max) pairs for linprog; minimize uses that exact same (min, max)-pair form: bounds=[(0.20, 0.60), (0.0, 1.2)].

slides.teaching: Reassure students this is not new syntax to memorize — the bounds argument looks identical to last week's linprog call.

slides.title: The exact same objective function as Week 9
slides.code:
import numpy as np
def basin(x: float, y: float, cx: float,
          cy: float, depth: float,
          wx: float, wy: float) -> float:
    """One Gaussian dip at (cx, cy), 'depth' deep."""
    return -depth * np.exp(-(((x-cx)**2)/(2*wx**2)
                             + ((y-cy)**2)/(2*wy**2)))
def energy_proxy(v: tuple) -> float:
    """Energy-use proxy at one (wwr, shade_m) pair."""
    w, s = v
    b1 = basin(w, s, 0.52, 0.25, 30.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    b2 = basin(w, s, 0.28, 0.90, 34.0, 0.06, 0.18)
    ridge = 6.0 * np.exp(-((w-0.40)**2)/0.02)
    return 20.0 + b1 + b2 + ridge
slides.explainHead: Nothing hidden: both functions, in full
slides.explainBody: This is exactly Week 9's two-basin energy_proxy, every line of it. basin() is a Gaussian dip: it returns a NEGATIVE number, deepest at (cx, cy), fading to zero far away. energy_proxy() adds two of them to a flat base of 20.0 — b1 near wwr=0.52 (30 deep) and b2 near wwr=0.28 (34 deep, the deeper one) — plus a ridge that raises the surface near wwr=0.40, walling the two basins apart. Both functions carry the one-line docstring and the parameter/return type hints this course has required since Week 4.
slides.teaching: Ask students to open their Week 9 handout side by side — every line here should look identical to what they already ran, now with the docstring and type hints spelled out. Read basin()'s signature aloud: seven floats in, one float out.

slides.title: ...continued: evaluate both basin centers
slides.code:
print('local basin center:',
      round(energy_proxy((0.52, 0.25)), 2))
print('lower basin center:',
      round(energy_proxy((0.28, 0.90)), 2))
gap = (energy_proxy((0.52, 0.25))
       - energy_proxy((0.28, 0.90)))
print('local basin is worse by:', round(gap, 2))
slides.output:
local basin center: -7.08
lower basin center: -11.08
local basin is worse by: 4.0
slides.explainBody: Calling energy_proxy at each basin center reproduces Week 9's numbers: -7.08 in the shallower basin and -11.08 in the lower basin. Their computed gap is 4.0 points. The lower basin is the best-known candidate from dense-grid plus multistart checks; those checks corroborate but do not prove continuous globality.
slides.teaching: Have students confirm these two numbers match their own Week 9 output. Name -11.08 the lower, best-corroborated basin rather than a proved global optimum.

slides.title: Gradient (slope), defined
slides.definition: At any point on the surface, the gradient is the direction and steepness of the fastest INCREASE. minimize reads it locally, then steps the opposite way — downhill — like a ball rolling down whatever slope is under it right now.

example.head: Why it does not see the whole surface
example.body: Week 9's grid sweep evaluated the ENTIRE surface, everywhere, before you ever looked at it. minimize does the opposite: it evaluates the slope only where it currently stands, moves one step, then reads the new local slope again.

slides.note: Gradient points toward locally steeper ground, not toward the true minimum — minimize only ever walks in the opposite direction from wherever it currently stands.
slides.teaching: Use a fog-on-a-hillside analogy: you can feel which way is downhill right where you stand, but you cannot see the next valley over.

slides.title: Initial guess (x0), defined
slides.definition: The (wwr, shade_m) pair handed to minimize as its starting point — the very first position on the surface the search ever evaluates. Every downhill step that follows is a chain reaction starting from exactly this one point.

example.head: Two demonstrations, one difference
example.body: Demo 1 starts at x0=(0.55, 0.20); Demo 2 starts at x0=(0.20, 1.00). Same energy_proxy, same bounds — x0 is the only argument that changes between them, and it is enough to change the reported answer by about four points.

slides.note: x0 is a deliberate choice made by whoever runs minimize — not a random pick, and not guaranteed to be a good one.
slides.teaching: Ask students where they would have started, before revealing two slides from now that most 'reasonable-looking' choices land in the wrong basin.

slides.title: The initial guess selects the first downhill path

steps.label: x0
steps.head: Choose a start
steps.body: A bounded WWR–shade pair begins the search.

steps.label: LOCAL SLOPE
steps.head: Read nearby change
steps.body: The solver estimates which nearby direction decreases the objective.

steps.label: STEP
steps.head: Move downhill
steps.body: A new point becomes the next local view of the surface.

steps.label: STOP
steps.head: Reach one basin
steps.body: Convergence can be clean even when another basin is lower.

slides.teaching: Treat x0 as part of the method, not a hidden convenience. The next two demonstrations differ only in the first node.

slides.title: Read the minimize() call one part at a time

parts.label: The function
parts.body: Gradient-based search from scipy.optimize — follows the slope downhill.

parts.label: The objective function
parts.body: The one function being minimized — must return a single number, like Week 10's objective.

parts.label: Starting guess
parts.body: Where the downhill walk begins — today's single biggest lever.

parts.label: Allowed range
parts.body: One (min, max) pair per variable — same form as Week 10's linprog.

slides.teaching: This is the general call shape; the real demo two slides from now substitutes an actual tuple for x0, e.g. x0=(0.55, 0.20). The next slide covers what comes back: result.x, result.fun, result.success.

slides.title: The result object, defined
slides.definition: minimize returns one result object with three fields worth reading every time: result.x is the (wwr, shade_m) pair it stopped at; result.fun is the objective value there; result.success reports whether the search converged cleanly — NOT whether it found the best point anywhere. Read all three together, never result.x alone.

example.head: Demo 1 and Demo 2, side by side
example.body: Both report success=True. Demo 1's result.fun is -7.1521 (the local trap); Demo 2's is -11.1437 (the lower best-known solution). Identical success flags, very different quality of answer.

slides.note: success == True feels like a green light. It only means the local search finished cleanly — never that this is the best possible answer anywhere in bounds.
slides.teaching: Point out result.success is True in both demonstrations coming next, even though one of them is the wrong answer — 'success' means the search converged, not that it found the best possible point.

slides.title: Predict before you run: does this start look safe?
slides.question: Which basin will x0=(0.55, 0.20) reach?
options: The lower best-known basin, value about -11.14
Exactly the local basin center, value -7.08
An error — x0 is outside bounds
slides.why: wwr=0.55 sits beside the local basin center (0.52, 0.25), so minimize follows the nearby slope and stops at -7.1521, not the deeper candidate.
slides.teaching: Ask: does x0=(0.55, 0.20) LOOK like a reasonable design guess? It should — that is exactly the trap. Take a show of hands on every option before revealing on the next slide.

slides.title: DEMO 1 — a plausible starting guess, minimize call
slides.code:
from scipy.optimize import minimize

bounds = [(0.20, 0.60), (0.0, 1.2)]

result = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.55, 0.20),
                  bounds=bounds)
print('x:', result.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result.fun, 4))
print('success:', result.success)
slides.explainBody: Starting at wwr=0.55, shade=0.20 — a plausible-looking design guess — minimize converges to wwr=0.5241, shade=0.2500, value=-7.1521. success is True: the search worked exactly as designed. It was simply never asked to look anywhere else.
slides.teaching: Ask: does this LOOK wrong? It should not — that is exactly the trap. Nothing about the printed output signals a problem.

slides.title: Local and global describe different comparison sets

steps.label: START A
steps.head: Nearby basin
steps.body: A downhill walk from (0.55, 0.20) reaches about −7.15.

steps.label: LOCAL
steps.head: No nearby improvement
steps.body: The solver legitimately stops at the bottom of that basin.

steps.label: START B
steps.head: Other side of ridge
steps.body: A second start reaches a different basin.

steps.label: CANDIDATE
steps.head: Lower, best known
steps.body: Dense-grid plus multistart evidence supports about −11.14, without proving globality.

slides.teaching: Write both values before the next run. Emphasize that success means convergence and numerical agreement means corroboration, not proof of the global minimum.

slides.title: Local optimum, defined
slides.definition: The best (lowest, here) value in a NEARBY region of the search space — better than every point immediately around it, but not necessarily the best value that exists further away.

example.head: Demo 1's result
example.body: Starting at (0.55, 0.20), minimize converges to (0.5241, 0.2500), value -7.1521. Every neighboring point really is worse — a genuine, reproducible local optimum, not a solver mistake.

slides.note: 'Local' does not mean small or unimportant — this basin is real and would look completely convincing if it were the only result computed.
slides.teaching: Contrast the definition with the next slide: a global optimum is best everywhere, while our numerical checks only corroborate a candidate.

slides.title: Global optimum, defined
slides.definition: The best value ANYWHERE inside the stated bounds — not just nearby, but compared against the entire feasible search space. There is only one global optimum value (ties aside), no matter how many local optima also exist.

example.head: A corroborated candidate, not a proof
example.body: Demo 2 reaches (0.2763, 0.9000), value -11.1437, close to Week 9's best point on an 81×61 grid (-11.135). Dense sampling plus multistart support this lower basin as the best-known candidate, but do not check every continuous point.

slides.note: minimize never proves its answer global. Multiple starts can expose a deeper basin; a finite sweep can corroborate a region. Neither alone is a proof over the continuum.
slides.teaching: Keep the definition of global optimum precise, then distinguish it from what these numerical checks establish: corroboration, not proof.

slides.title: Predict before you run: only x0 changes
slides.question: Same function, same bounds. Only x0 moved. Which basin now?
options: Still the local optimum, -7.1521 — x0 barely matters
A THIRD, new optimum somewhere between the two
The same as Demo 1, since minimize always returns one fixed answer
slides.why: (0.20, 1.00) sits near the lower basin center (0.28, 0.90); minimize converges to (0.2763, 0.9000), value -11.1437. Only x0 changed.
slides.teaching: Option D names the exact misconception this whole lesson corrects — minimize is deterministic for a fixed function, method, and start, but a different start can reach a different basin.

slides.title: DEMO 2 — only x0 changes
slides.code:
result2 = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.20, 1.00),
                   bounds=bounds)
print('x:', result2.x.round(4))
print('value:', round(result2.fun, 4))
print('success:', result2.success)
slides.explainHead: Same function. Same bounds. Different answer.
slides.explainBody: Only x0 changed. This run reaches the lower basin at wwr=0.2763, shade=0.9000, value=-11.1437 — the best result found in this multi-start plus dense-grid check. Agreement with Week 9's sampled minimum corroborates the result; it does not prove the continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Let this land in silence for a second before moving on — same three lines of code as Demo 1, one argument changed, four points of energy proxy recovered. Name it the lower, best-corroborated basin rather than claiming a proof of globality.

slides.title: Recorded objective values never rise
slides.chartTitle: Recorded objective value at each solver callback
slides.explainBody: In these two callback traces, the accepted objective decreases or stays flat. Start A settles near -7.15; its final plotted point is repeated only to align the axes. Start B settles near -11.14. This describes these recorded accepted iterates — not a promise that every solver's internal trial path is strictly monotone.
slides.teaching: Both traces use scipy's callback on the exact Demo 1/2 calls. Start A has 6 real recorded values and one repeated alignment point; Start B has 7 real values. Distinguish plotted accepted iterates from unshown internal trial steps.

slides.title: Eight starting guesses, one verified pattern
slides.callout: 5 of 8 plausible starting guesses land in the WORSE local optimum; 3 reach the lower candidate.
slides.teaching: This is the verified multistart table. LOWER means best among these corroborating checks, not a proof over the continuum.

slides.title: The code behind that table: one multistart function
slides.explainHead: The whole workflow, wrapped in one function
slides.explainBody: Nothing new is being computed here — this is the previous table, written as code you could run on any objective. fn is a FUNCTION passed in as an argument, exactly the way energy_proxy is already handed to minimize. The loop runs one minimize per starting guess, rounds the objective, and keeps a running best in a dict. -9 sits deliberately between the two verified values (-7.1521 and -11.1437), so 'value > -9' counts the local-trap runs — a labeling convenience for THIS verified problem, not a general rule.
slides.teaching: Point out that this is the first function in the course that takes another function as an argument — and that students have already been doing it every time they wrote minimize(energy_proxy, ...). Trace the two if-statements out loud: one counts, one remembers.

slides.title: ...continued: run it on all eight starting guesses
slides.code:
STARTS = [(0.55, 0.20), (0.50, 0.30), (0.40, 0.55),
          (0.45, 0.60), (0.60, 0.10), (0.20, 1.00),
          (0.30, 0.85), (0.22, 1.15)]
best = multistart(energy_proxy, STARTS, bounds)
print('best start:', best['start'])
print('best x:', best['x'])
print('best value:', best['value'])
slides.output:
LOCAL trap: 5 of 8
best start: (0.2, 1.0)
best x: [0.2763 0.9   ]
best value: -11.1437
slides.explainHead: The table's headline, computed instead of read
slides.explainBody: Eight minimize calls, one printed summary: 5 of the 8 land in the local trap, and the best run of all eight started at (0.20, 1.00) and reached wwr=0.2763, shade=0.9000, value=-11.1437. Reporting only best['value'] would hide the 5-of-8 split entirely — which is exactly why multistart() prints the count as well as returning the winner. Meeting B rebuilds this same sweep as a pandas table.
slides.teaching: Ask what would be lost if this function returned only the best result and printed nothing: the answer would still be right, but the evidence that a single run is untrustworthy would disappear.

slides.title: 5 of 8 land in the trap, visualized
slides.explainHead: Same eight rows, one bar chart
slides.explainBody: Five of eight starts land in the worse local optimum; three reach the lower best-known basin. The label reports relative evidence from these runs, not a proof that the lower basin is globally optimal over every continuous point.
slides.teaching: Ask which bar students expected to be taller. Reinforce that frequency and objective quality differ, and that LOWER means best corroborated here, not proved global.

slides.title: Why the starting guess changes the answer

left.head: What minimize can see
left.body: Local information near its current position. If that information points toward the shallower basin, it can settle there without discovering a deeper basin elsewhere.

right.head: What Week 9's sweep could see
right.body: All 4,941 nodes in a fixed 81×61 grid at once. That gives broad sampled coverage, while minimize trades coverage for speed. Neither method here checks every continuous point.

slides.teaching: Frame the trade-off as local efficiency versus sampled coverage, then repeat: a finite grid corroborates a region but does not prove globality over the continuum.

slides.title: The cost of sampled coverage vs. local search
rows: best sampled grid value; not the continuum
a converged local result; no global certificate
slides.callout: The grid buys broad sampled coverage at higher cost; local search buys speed but can stop in a worse basin. Neither computation alone proves the continuous global optimum.
slides.teaching: Use the verified evaluation counts, then distinguish sampled coverage, local convergence, and a true global-optimality certificate.

slides.title: Predict before you run: no bounds argument at all
slides.code:
result_a = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.0, 0.0))
result_b = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(1.0, 1.0))
slides.question: With no bounds= argument, what does each run report?
options: Both succeed, but at physically meaningless x values
Both converge back into the lower basin anyway
A warning, but the same values as the bounded runs
slides.why: Both report success=True. Far from either basin the surface is nearly flat, so minimize stops where it stands: wwr=-0.1974 and wwr=1.0.
slides.teaching: bounds is an optional argument to minimize, not a required one — that is exactly why leaving it off does not error, and exactly why it should never be left off on a real design problem.

slides.title: Why bounds matter: unbounded runs can go nowhere useful
slides.code:
# no bounds= argument at all
result_a = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(0.0, 0.0))
print('start (0.0, 0.0) ->', result_a.x.round(4),
      round(result_a.fun, 4))

result_b = minimize(energy_proxy, x0=(1.0, 1.0))
print('start (1.0, 1.0) ->', result_b.x.round(4),
      round(result_b.fun, 4))
slides.explainBody: wwr=-0.1974 is a negative window-to-wall ratio; wwr=1.0 with no bounds check is an all-glass wall accepted without question. Both runs report success because far from either basin the surface is nearly flat — minimize has no slope to follow, so it stops wherever it happens to be standing.
slides.teaching: Run this live if time allows — result.success is True for both, which is exactly why success alone is not enough to trust a result.

slides.title: Bounds, defined (for minimize)

left.head: Same idea, same syntax as Week 10
left.body: bounds=[(0.20, 0.60), (0.0, 1.2)] — one (min, max) pair per design variable, identical in form to linprog's bounds argument.

right.head: A different job here
right.body: Week 10's bounds capped a structural limit (solar area ≤ 120 m2). Here, bounds keeps wwr and shade_m inside the physically buildable envelope — and, as the previous slide showed, keeps the solver from wandering into a flat region with no signal at all.

slides.teaching: Connect back explicitly to the unbounded demo just shown — bounds is not optional politeness, it is what keeps the answer physically real.

slides.title: The minimize workflow, every time

steps.label: DEFINE
steps.head: Write the objective
steps.body: One function returning a single number to minimize, exactly like energy_proxy(v).

steps.label: BOUNDS
steps.head: State the physical range
steps.body: One (min, max) pair per design variable — keeps every candidate buildable.

steps.label: GUESS
steps.head: Choose x0
steps.body: Pick a starting point — and know on a nonlinear problem it might not be enough.

steps.label: VERIFY
steps.head: Try a second, different x0
steps.body: Compare results before trusting either one — agreement is reassurance, disagreement is real information.

slides.teaching: This four-step order is the procedural takeaway students should be able to recite before Wednesday's studio.

slides.title: Combining Week 9 and Week 11

left.head: Sweep, then refine
left.body: Week 9's grid sweep is slow but sees everything; minimize is fast but sees only its own neighborhood. Used together: sweep first (or scan a handful of spread-out starting guesses) to find promising regions, THEN run minimize from inside each region to refine each promising candidate.

right.head: This is real practice, not busywork
right.body: Nobody trusts a single minimize run on a genuinely nonlinear problem. Project 2 Part II requires trying at least two different initial guesses and reporting whether they agree — exactly today's demonstration, applied to your own problem.

slides.teaching: Preview Meeting B's studio: students will build the same multi-start table shown today, then write the required agreement/disagreement finding.

slides.title: Transfer the multistart test: courtyard width × opening ratio
slides.prompt: A nonlinear comfort–daylight proxy has two bounded variables and may contain more than one low region.
steps: Choose three physically different starting guesses within the same bounds.
Run minimize from each start and record success, variables, and objective value.
Compare agreement or disagreement; verify every returned candidate against bounds.
Translate the best and alternate basins into distinct architectural implications.
slides.teaching: No fixed numeric answer is required; the evidence is the multistart table. Students should distinguish a narrow/deep courtyard solution from a wider/lower-opening alternative only if the proxy and returned values support that wording. Agreement is reassuring but not proof of global optimality; disagreement is a finding. Require the same objective and bounds across starts so only the initial condition changes.

slides.title: Why this matters for Project 2

left.head: Two required, non-optional families
left.body: Project 2 Part II requires BOTH linprog (Week 10) and minimize (Week 11) — solve your linear sub-component exactly, then solve the full nonlinear objective by search, trying at least two different initial guesses.

right.head: What 'reporting' means
right.body: State whether your two starting guesses agree. If they don't — exactly like today's demonstration — that disagreement IS the finding, not a mistake to hide, and belongs directly in your one-page solver card.

slides.teaching: Name the solver card explicitly here for the first time — Meeting B will define it fully.

slides.title: The starting guess is part of the answer
takeaways: minimize follows local information from your initial guess; it never sees the full continuum.
A local optimum is real and reproducible; a lower basin may exist elsewhere in bounds.
5 of 8 plausible starts land at -7.1521; only 3 reach the lower best-known basin at -11.1437.
Dense-grid plus multistart agreement is useful corroboration, not proof of globality.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: write one next starting guess, predict its basin, and state what the result can and cannot establish.
